verses.text: Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus.
When they were at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. They had also John as their attendant.
When they had gone through the island to Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar Jesus,
who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summoned Barnabas and Saul, and sought to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn aside the proconsul from the faith.
But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastened his eyes on him,
and said, “Full of all deceit and all cunning, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!” Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos, and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.
But they, passing on from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia. They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down.
After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.”
Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand said, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people  chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it.
For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance, for about four hundred fifty years.
After these things he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.
Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’
From this man’s offspring,  God has brought salvation  to Israel according to his promise,
before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel.
As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, one comes after me the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’
Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you.
For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed.
When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.
We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers,
that God has fulfilled the same to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father.’
“Concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’
Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see decay.’
For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep, and was laid with his fathers, and saw decay.
But he whom God raised up saw no decay.
Be it known to you therefore, brothers,  that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins,
and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets:
‘Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work which you will in no way believe, if one declares it to you.’”
So when the Jews went out of the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these words might be preached to them the next Sabbath.
Now when the synagogue broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
The next Sabbath almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God.
But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with jealousy, and contradicted the things which were spoken by Paul, and blasphemed.

Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, and said, “It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.
For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’”
As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
The Lord’s word was spread abroad throughout all the region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, and stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and threw them out of their borders.
But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium.
The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

footnotes.content: The Spirit's work always begins with willing vessels in the ordinary gathering—teachers, prophets, men of different stations all gathered in one room at Antioch. Notice Barnabas is named first; his steadiness sets the tone. And then there's Saul, the same man who held cloaks at Stephen's stoning. The Lord wasn't waiting for perfect people; He was waiting for open hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Holy Spirit speaks *during* worship and fasting—when the mind is quiet and the heart is surrendered. "Separate Barnabas and Saul for me" is not a gentle suggestion but a divine assignment. The Spirit doesn't ask permission; He declares the work that is already His. Notice the certainty: He has already called them; now their friends must release them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prayer, fasting, the laying on of hands—the church sends them off not with fanfare but with intercession and blessing. This is how the faithful release the called: with time on their knees, not with words of doubt. What a gift their sending was; two people going out held up by the prayers of their assembly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Sent out by the Holy Spirit"—this phrase settles everything. Men's hands might commission, but the Spirit drives. They went to Seleucia first, then sailed to Cyprus. The path was clear, not because they had a map, but because the One who calls also guides each step forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Salamis they proclaimed the word in the Jewish synagogues—beginning with their own people, as tradition required. Young John goes as their helper, learning by watching Barnabas and Paul proclaim Jesus in the very places where the Law was read each Sabbath. Sometimes the best apprenticeship is standing near faith in action.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They crossed the island to Paphos and found a sorcerer, a false prophet. The enemy works through deception—promising sight, peddling lies. The Lord always lets us meet the resistance head-on, so we learn His power isn't just over our own hearts, but over the principalities that deceive the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sergius Paulus was a man of understanding—someone hungry for truth beneath the surface. How often the Lord places seekers in positions of power, waiting for His messengers to arrive. The sorcerer was attached to him, but Jesus draws the honest heart toward light. Bar Jesus feared what Paul might reveal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elymas—the name means "wise" in Arabic, a title the sorcerer wore like a badge. But the Spirit showed his true nature: one bent on turning seekers away from the Lord. The greatest opposition to the Gospel often comes dressed in the language of knowledge and power, offering false comfort for a true hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Saul becomes Paul in Scripture—his Roman name emerging as he stands before the proconsul. "Filled with the Holy Spirit," he fixes his gaze. There's no doubt, no hesitation. He sees clearly what needs to be named. The Spirit doesn't leave us foggy when truth must be defended.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks harshly, naming deception and enmity. This isn't cruelty—it's clarity. "You son of the devil," echoing Jesus's own words to those who resist His kingdom. The Spirit equips His servants sometimes not with honey, but with truth that cuts. The one who perverts righteousness faces righteousness unblunted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hand of the Lord touched the sorcerer with blindness—not permanent judgment, but a sign, immediate and undeniable. Darkness fell on Elymas as surely as grace had fallen on Paul years before. The proconsul would see this and understand: the Gospel speaks not in boasts but in acts, and the God of Jesus commands creation itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sergius Paulus believed, amazed at the teaching of the Lord—but amazed *by* what he saw first. The miracle opened his eyes. Often the seeking heart needs not just words but a sign that what is being preached is not mere philosophy, but the presence of living power. One man's openness led him from darkness into light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Paphos they sailed to Perga in Pamphylia—the journey continues. But John left them and returned to Jerusalem. We don't judge him harshly; his heart may have failed, or his calling lay elsewhere. Not every companion walks the full distance. The Spirit appoints some for seasons, others for the long haul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Antioch of Pisidia they entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down—the custom respected, the moment ripe. They didn't force their way to speak; they waited, known to the pattern of worship. Sometimes witness begins simply by being present, sitting quietly among the people, showing that following Jesus doesn't separate us from our own faith's roots.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the law and prophets were read, the rulers invited them to speak—hospitality to visitors was the custom. What grace in those Sabbath rules; a stranger's voice was welcome if it could edify. Paul didn't seize the moment; the Spirit prepared the open door. One phrase—"if you have a word of exhortation"—and the way was made for the Gospel to speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul stood, gestured, and addressed them not as critics but as brothers and God-fearers. His tone was respectful, inviting them to listen as equals. The Spirit's boldness in Paul never became rudeness; he met people where they were—steeped in Scripture, hungry for truth—and spoke to that hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul traced God's choice of Abraham's seed, then the exaltation in Egypt and the exodus with an uplifted arm. He began where they all began—with the foundational story, God's steadfast choosing and powerful deliverance. Not to condemn their history, but to show that the same God who led then is leading now, and His purpose was always moving toward something greater.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years in the wilderness—the Lord endured their grumbling, their doubt, their rebellion. Even when we wander, even when we test His patience, He bears with us like a parent with a wayward child. This wasn't only history; it was a mirror held up to the hearts listening: God's patience toward His people is inexhaustible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven nations destroyed, the land given as inheritance for four hundred fifty years. The Lord cleared the way for His people; He didn't leave them wandering but gave them a home. Each promise fulfilled, each boundary established—the pattern showed that God finishes what He begins. Every chapter of Israel was written by a faithful Hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judges led them until Samuel—leaders raised up for seasons of need. The Lord didn't abandon Israel to chaos; He provided shepherds, though imperfect ones. Samuel marked the turning point, the threshold between judges and kings, between the scattered tribes and a unified kingdom. Every age had its appointed guide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They asked for a king, and God gave them Saul of Benjamin for forty years. The people wanted what other nations had; the Lord gave it, though it wasn't His ideal. Sometimes He grants our requests knowing they'll teach us what we needed to learn. Saul's reign would reveal both the gift and the limitation of ruling without God's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul failed, God raised David—a man after His heart, one who would do His will. The promise was a change of dynasty but not a change of purpose; God's kingdom would continue through David's line, not because of David's perfection, but because of the Lord's covenant mercy. The seed was planted; the promise pointed forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From David's offspring came salvation for Israel according to promise. Every verse Paul recited was leading them here—to the realization that their entire history, all those judges and kings and wanderings, was a story pointing toward One. The genealogy wasn't mere memory; it was a map, and Jesus was the destination it marked all along.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before Jesus came, John preached baptism of repentance. The forerunner prepared the way; hearts softened by his call were ready to receive the Messiah. John was the last of the prophets and the first to bow before the One the prophets had promised. His voice made the way straight for feet that would change everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John spoke his own unworthiness: "I am not he; one comes after me whose sandal laces I am not worthy to untie." Even a forerunner born of the Spirit knew his place—not the center, but the herald. The humility of John's witness is the humility of all true servants: to rejoice in being the friend who introduces the Bridegroom, knowing the marriage is not ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Children of Abraham's stock, and you who fear God"—Paul addressed them all: the born Jews and the Gentiles drawn to their faith. The word of salvation was sent to *them*, in their synagogue, in that hour. No one listening could escape the claim; this promise was not historical whisper but present fire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rulers in Jerusalem didn't know Him; they couldn't see that the prophets read every Sabbath were speaking of Jesus. Blindness came not from ignorance but from closed hearts. The very words that should have prepared them became a mirror they refused to look into. How often truth hides in plain sight, waiting for eyes willing to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Though they found no cause for death, they asked Pilate to kill Jesus. Injustice spoke against the innocent with false witness and political expedience. The powers of this world can demand death even when judgment finds no guilt. Yet Paul reminds them: this too was written, foreknown, woven into the very purposes of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb—the humiliation complete, the story seemingly ended. Yet every step, even the ignominy, fulfilled what was written. The darkness of the tomb, the silence of the grave—all of it was part of the pathway to resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But God raised Him from the dead—three words that undo all defeat, that break the silence, that remake everything. Death could not contain Him because He is the Author of life. This is where all of history pivoted: one Man rises, and the covenant is fulfilled not in shadow but in reality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He appeared for many days to those from Galilee who came up with Him to Jerusalem—witnesses who saw Him eat, walk, speak, alive in a body. The resurrection wasn't vision or hallucination; it was concrete, seen by people who knew Him and couldn't be deceived. These witnesses would testify at great cost. They saw; they knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers"—Paul shifts from history to proclamation. Everything he recited wasn't mere narrative; it was foundation for the good news he now declared. The prophets, the judges, the kings, the coming one—all of it finds its fulfillment in the One before them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God fulfilled the promise to their children by raising Jesus—not as a prophet, but as Son. The psalm declared it: "You are my Son; today I have become your father." The resurrection was God's fatherly pronouncement, His way of saying *Yes* to the One He loved, *Amen* to all He had promised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God raised Him no more to return to corruption—this is the guarantee written into the psalm itself. Christ's resurrection is not like others' who rose only to die again; His is final, settled, beyond decay. He entered a new kind of existence altogether, the first fruits of the kingdom that death cannot touch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You will not allow Your Holy One to see decay"—another psalm, another stone laid in the testimony. Scripture itself testifies that the Messiah would be raised, preserved, held by the Father's hand. Every verse Paul quoted was written centuries before and spoke directly to the Man standing there in memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David served God's counsel in his generation, then fell asleep with his fathers and saw decay—a king, yes, but mortal. His bones are dust. He was faithful, but he was not the final word. The lineage mattered because it led somewhere; David's throne was preparation for a throne that cannot be shaken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But He whom God raised saw no decay—the contrast is absolute and final. Jesus is not one more link in the chain; He is the fulfillment of the chain itself. His body didn't return to dust; it was raised transformed, alive beyond the reach of corruption. This is the difference between a great ancestor and the Messiah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Through this Man, remission of sins is proclaimed to you—the centerpiece of the Gospel. All that went before leads to this: not that sins are overlooked, but that they are genuinely forgiven through trust in the risen Jesus. This is the word the synagogue needed to hear, and still needs to hear today.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By Him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses—Paul draws the line clear and kind. The law showed us our need but couldn't wash us clean; Jesus washes and restores. This is why the Gospel is good news, not demand; it offers what the law could never give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets"—Paul warns gently. The choice was theirs: believe the good news or remain under judgment. He quoted Habakkuk, speaking of those who scoff and perish, those who cannot believe even when the work of God is declared to them. The stakes were real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days which you will in no way believe if one declares it to you." The ancient prophet spoke as if to that very moment—a work so great the mind reels at it, so unlikely that those who hear might refuse it even as it unfolds. God works; faith recognizes; refusal watches the work pass by.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Jews left the synagogue, the Gentiles begged to hear Paul's words the next Sabbath. The outsiders hungered for what the insiders didn't yet embrace. So often those we think farthest from God's truth are closest to the truth when it's faithfully spoken. The hungry heart, wherever it dwells, reaches toward light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many Jews and devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, urged to continue in the grace of God. Not all refused; some believed. The apostles spoke to them gently, calling them to hold fast to grace itself—not a system, not a performance, but the unearned favor of God poured out toward them in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God—the movement spread like leaven. One sermon, faithfully preached, stirred the city's curiosity. People brought their friends; the hungry invited the hungry; word took root. The Gospel has always spread this way: one person telling another, "Come and see."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But when the Jews saw the multitudes, jealousy filled them and they contradicted Paul, blaspheming. Opposition born of fear, contradicted by truth they couldn't refute, so they resorted to insult. Every movement toward Jesus has provoked this response—not always argument, sometimes rage. Those threatened by light grow loud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly: God's word should be spoken to you first; since you reject it, we turn to the Gentiles. The offer was refused by those first invited; grace then turned to the second door. This was not rejection of God's preference for Israel, but recognition that the kingdom expands where it is received. Not spite, but gospel logic.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord commanded, "I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth." Paul quoted Isaiah—a prophecy about the Servant, now applied to the apostles' calling. They were not acting outside God's word but fulfilling it. Every generation is a light-bearer; the darkness is wide, and God's vision is for the whole earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gentiles heard this and were glad, glorified God's word, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. There's mystery and simplicity together: as many as the Lord appointed believed. Faith is a response to good news, yet only those *set for* faith receive it truly. The Lord's sovereignty and human choice embrace both truths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's word spread throughout the region—not by force or promotion, but by the power of truth received and carried forward. One city, then ripples. One faithful witness, then multitudes. This is always how the Gospel moves: *logos* becomes *debar*—the word becomes deed, becomes speech, becomes transformed lives talking to other lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the Jews stirred up devout women and prominent men to drive Paul and Barnabas out of the city. Opposition mobilized allies, weaponized propriety. Persecution was dressed in civic duty. The apostles faced not random violence but organized removal by the city itself. Yet even this fulfilled their course—forward, always forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They shook off the dust of their feet against the city and went to Iconium—the ancient gesture of rejection, done without bitterness. No bending backward, no looking to negotiate. When a place says no, faithful servants shake the dust and continue. The seed was planted; whether it grows is not their charge, but the Lord's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit—and here I see something that makes my heart turn even now, looking back from a longer road. Expelled, rejected, driven from the city they'd entered in hope, yet *full of joy*. Not bitterness, not defeat, but gladness that the Spirit had not withdrawn. Readers today hear an echo in this: the world can take much, but it cannot take the Father's joy from those who belong to Him. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful that joy is not the world's to grant or deny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
